question: Can a Transformer generate outputs equivariant to arbitrary renamings of interchangeable symbols and extend to more symbols than were seen in training without learning one embedding per symbol, while retaining enough identity information to solve relational formal-logic tasks?

key_findings.claim: The architecture replaces per-symbol learned embeddings with one parallel shared-weight stream per distinct interchangeable input symbol and uses symmetric aggregation to make renaming act only as a stream permutation.
key_findings.evidence: For k distinct interchangeable tokens in an input, stream i embeds occurrences of token i with one learned 'actual' row and every other interchangeable token with one learned placeholder row; non-interchangeable tokens are unchanged. Encoder and decoder operations share weights across streams. Per-stream attention preserves identity, aggregate-view attention communicates across identities, decoder cross-attention can use corresponding or aggregated encoder streams, and projection averages base-token logits while taking interchangeable-token i's logit from stream i. The learned embedding table therefore has only V_n+2 rows while the dynamic output contains V_n+k symbols.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes alpha-equivariance, despite the paper's recurring 'invariant' terminology: renaming an input renames a symbol-valued output rather than leaving it literally unchanged.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem states that for alpha-renaming f and model M, if y-hat=M(x) and y-hat'=M(f(x)), then f^{-1}(y-hat')=y-hat, equivalently y-hat'=f(y-hat). The proof tracks the induced stream permutation, shared per-stream operations, commutative aggregation, and stream-indexed projection. This is the appropriate covariance/equivariance property for assignments and traces whose output symbol names should follow the input; literal invariance holds only after de-renaming or for fixed-vocabulary outputs.

key_findings.claim: The proof is convincing for the stated stream operations under a fixed bijection, but does not fully formalize end-to-end autoregressive decoding or every practical source of exact covariance.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B proves equivariance of embeddings, layers, aggregation, and logits under a stream permutation. It does not explicitly give an induction over generated prefixes, define how a dynamically expanded V_i' relates to stream creation when symbols are absent, or handle greedy/beam tie-breaking, stochastic-sampling coupling, floating-point reduction order, dropout, and padding/batching masks. These omissions do not refute the layerwise result, but perfect sequence-level equality requires deterministic equivariant decoding or coupled randomness and implementation details beyond the written theorem.

key_findings.claim: On the main renamed and reduced-data comparisons, the proposed model improves validator correctness and is exactly alpha-covariant across tested permutations.
key_findings.evidence: For propositional logic on the renamed training set, correct/exact rates are 98.03%/60.96% for the proposal versus 93.85%/57.24% for alpha-renaming embeddings and 93.25%/56.45% for random dual-part embeddings; on the 80k reduced set they are 70.43%/35.81% versus 57.48%/26.77% and 55.23%/26.28%. For LTL, renamed results are 98.24%/79.65% versus 97.96%/77.66% and 95.94%/76.45%; reduced results are 93.46%/68.63% versus 89.50%/64.15% and 87.32%/59.04%. The proposed model reports 100% alpha-covariance at 3, 4, and 5 APs in every regime.

key_findings.claim: The claimed in-distribution/OOD Pareto improvement is confounded by training-data preprocessing because the proposal is not evaluated on the same normal-data regime as the fixed-vocabulary baseline.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 compares the standard baseline trained on the normal 800k set (95.62% propositional correctness, 98.23% LTL) with the proposal trained on a renamed/canonicalized 800k set (98.03%, 98.24%). Canonicalization orders atomic propositions by first appearance, changing the distribution and reducing irrelevant name-order variation. There is no proposed-model row trained on the normal set, nor a standard baseline with identical dynamic architecture and data. Therefore the architecture, canonicalization, and vocabulary treatment cannot be disentangled in the claim that the proposal surpasses the normal baseline in and out of distribution.

key_findings.claim: Alpha-covariance measures prediction consistency under renaming, not correctness or proof of the theorem by itself.
key_findings.evidence: For all alpha-equivalent inputs P, outputs are de-renamed and U is the set of distinct predictions; the score is 1-(|U|-1)/(|P|-1). A model that emits the same fixed-vocabulary or constant output for every permutation can score 1 even when wrong, and the expression is undefined for |P|=1. Table 1 appropriately reports validator correctness separately, but the statement that perfect empirical alpha-covariance 'validates Theorem 4.1' overstates finite testing: all permutations are checked only for 1,000 sampled inputs (100 for GPT-5.2) at selected AP counts.

key_findings.claim: The out-of-distribution heatmaps favor the proposal strongly on propositional logic but show only a small or absent advantage on LTL, a disclosed negative result tied to the task bottleneck.
key_findings.evidence: Training uses at most 5 APs and formula length 35; the heatmap extends to 10 APs and length 50 with at most 100 items per cell. Mean propositional heatmap correctness is 95.05% for the proposal versus 84.41% for full vocabulary, 69.96% for alpha-renaming, and 77.70% for random embeddings. LTL results cluster at 90.47%, 92.82%, 90.13%, and 87.70%, so the full-vocabulary baseline is actually higher. The authors attribute this to temporal reasoning, rather than AP-relationship handling, being the LTL bottleneck. The Figure 2 caption reverses the top/bottom task order relative to its panel labels: the top is labeled propositional logic and the bottom LTL.

key_findings.claim: Architecture selection uses a 10-AP validation set even though training stops at 5 APs, creating target-distribution exposure in the claimed open-vocabulary generalization evaluation.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5.5 says the best configuration for each task was selected by hyperparameter tuning on a separate validation set with 10 APs; the main generalization axis is precisely extrapolation from at most 5 training APs to up to 10 APs. The heatmap test set is distinct, so this is not direct test-set reuse, but model selection has access to labeled examples at the maximum target vocabulary size. Performance therefore demonstrates OOD generalization after OOD-aware selection, not zero-exposure extrapolation to 10 symbols.

key_findings.claim: Per-stream decoder and cross-attention are essential in these tasks, while aggregated attention is task dependent and can hurt, so the paper's broad claim that both mechanisms are complementary needs qualification.
key_findings.evidence: For propositional logic, the best EP-DP-EA-DA-CP configuration scores 95.05%; replacing CP with aggregate CA collapses to 28.51%, removing DP to 46.55%, removing DA to 84.48%, removing EA to 92.47%, and removing both aggregate paths to 72.35%. For LTL, best EP-DP-EA-CP is 90.47%; replacing CP with CA collapses to 20.93%, but adding CA slightly lowers accuracy to 90.27%, adding DA lowers it to 89.47%, and removing all aggregate attention still achieves 84.13%. Per-stream routing is consistently vital; decoder aggregation is beneficial only for the relational propositional task and is mildly negative for LTL.

key_findings.claim: The GPT-5.2 comparison contextualizes specialized-model performance but is not a controlled basis for claiming general superiority.
key_findings.evidence: GPT-5.2 with medium reasoning, four-shot infix prompts, temperature 0, and JSON constraints scores 99.73% propositional correctness but only 25.60% exact match, and 86.83%/35.93% on LTL. Its heatmap scores are 99.49% propositional and 81.45% LTL. Financial constraints reduce GPT heatmaps from 100 to 10 items per cell, Table 1 from 100k to 3k test samples, and covariance from 1,000 to 100; no confidence intervals are reported. The specialized model's top-10/top-25 beam accuracy of 99.03%/99.54% is compared with GPT's single response, so candidate compute and sample counts are unmatched. GPT takes 10-90 seconds per response, averaging 37 seconds on 387 sequential LTL items, but API and local-hardware latency are also not hardware matched.

key_findings.claim: The approach is open-vocabulary only in the bounded extrapolation sense and scales linearly in the number of input symbols on top of quadratic sequence attention.
key_findings.evidence: With S streams and length L, inference time is O(SL^2) and activation memory O(SLd). On propositional logic, reported single-sample time grows from 3.38 ms to 5.13 ms from 1 to 10 APs; on the LTL heatmap at batch 64, activation memory grows from 1.9 GB at 5 APs to 3.9 GB at 10, versus 3.1 to 3.2 GB for full vocabulary. Only S<=10 is tested. The authors explicitly state that hundreds of local variables may be prohibitive, symbol streams are instantiated only for input symbols, and the model cannot invent a fresh interchangeable output token. The k=0 implementation creates one dummy stream and cannot output an interchangeable token.

anchors.section: Appendix A / Edge case: no interchangeable tokens

key_findings.claim: The conversion experiment shows useful initialization transfer to a restricted per-stream model, but does not demonstrate that a general pretrained Transformer gains the full proposed architecture or fully recovers its original performance with minimal fine-tuning.
key_findings.evidence: Conversion disables all aggregated attention, maps two existing symbol embeddings to actual/placeholder rows, and copies the remaining weights into EP-DP-CP. On propositional logic, a pretrained 5-AP baseline scores 95.57%; after one/five epochs, converted models score 87.54%/90.55% at 5 AP, 67.17%/68.78% at 10 AP, and 70.11%/71.35% on the heatmap, versus 91.47%/69.97%/72.35% from scratch. Thus five epochs do not recover the original in-distribution 95.57%, and conversion excludes the best model's aggregate layers. On LTL, one epoch does exceed the from-scratch restricted model on the heatmap (85.91% versus 84.13%) while remaining below pretrained in-distribution accuracy (94.75% versus 97.96%). The 'existing pretrained model' is a small task-specific encoder-decoder, not a general LLM.

key_findings.claim: Several evaluations are nondiscriminating or undercontrolled: copying saturates, LTL is bottlenecked elsewhere, and model configurations differ without seed-level uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: On the scalable-copy task, all methods obtain edit distance 0 across the tested length/vocabulary grid after training on 10 million strings, so it provides no evidence favoring the proposal. LTL heatmaps place full vocabulary above the proposal and show tightly clustered methods. Hyperparameters and parameter counts differ across methods and tasks (for example proposed LTL uses embedding 64/4 heads whereas baselines use 128/8; selected models span about 2.46-3.13M parameters), based on preliminary tuning. No number of random seeds, variance, confidence interval, or statistical test is reported anywhere in the tables.

anchors.section: Appendix D / Table 5 and Appendix E / Copying

key_findings.claim: The LTL result depends on a targeted training-set rebalance drawn from another baseline's training corpus, which is disclosed but adds a dataset-construction dependency.
key_findings.evidence: The original LTL set contains only one 0-AP and 11,635 1-AP examples. The authors add formulas from the full-vocabulary baseline training set to reach 203 and 22,474, then retrain all models and state that no augmented item overlaps evaluation. Heatmap accuracy improves from 82.71% to 90.15% for the alpha-renaming baseline. This is not reported test leakage, but it means final LTL performance is conditional on a manual rare-regime rebalance and is not directly the original prior-work training distribution.

method.core_idea: Represent symbol identity relationally rather than with a permanent name embedding: make one shared-weight view for each symbol present in the input, ensure renaming merely reorders those views, and restrict every cross-view operation to permutation-equivariant or permutation-invariant aggregation.
method.mechanism: Partition the vocabulary into fixed base tokens V_n and interchangeable tokens V_i. At runtime enumerate the k distinct interchangeable input symbols. In stream i, replace symbol i by an actual-symbol index V_n and every other interchangeable symbol by placeholder index V_n+1, retaining a mask for symbol i's positions. Apply shared per-stream encoder/decoder attention. Construct an aggregate view by averaging all streams and restoring each symbol's own-stream state at its masked positions; optionally attend to this view in encoder and decoder. Decoder cross-attention uses corresponding encoder streams or the aggregate. At projection, average base-token logits across streams and take dynamic symbol i's logit from stream i's actual-symbol row. A bijective alpha-renaming permutes stream/mask order, so shared operations commute with it and aggregation is unchanged.
assumptions: The interchangeable-token partition is given correctly in advance and all members are genuinely symmetric except for identity relations.
Alpha-renaming is a bijection that fixes base tokens and preserves scope/meaning; capture, binding scope, and contextual differences are outside the formalization.
Every interchangeable symbol that may be generated already appears in the encoder input so that a corresponding stream exists.
The number of distinct input symbols is small enough that O(SL^2) time and O(SLd) activation memory are practical.
Shared parameters, commutative aggregation, masks, batching, and decoding are implemented without identity-dependent branches that break equivariance.
Renamed/canonicalized training data and 10-AP validation examples are acceptable supervision for assessing post-training open-vocabulary generalization.
Satisfying-assignment and LTL validators correctly score all semantically valid outputs; exact string match is secondary because witnesses are non-unique.
Synthetic propositional and LTL tasks with at most ten symbols are representative enough to motivate code/theorem-proving extensions.

techniques.role: Creates one dynamic view per distinct interchangeable input symbol using only two learned symbol embedding rows.
Processes symbol views independently with common weights so renaming permutes outputs rather than changing computations.
Averages views and restores each symbol's own representation at its occurrences to expose a symmetric relational context.
Lets decoder streams either align with the corresponding encoder symbol or attend to a symmetric aggregate; ablations show correspondence is crucial.
Averages fixed-vocabulary logits and routes each dynamic symbol logit from its matching stream.
De-renames predictions over all tested symbol permutations and scores whether they collapse to one output.
Uses pyaiger for propositional assignments and Spot 2.11.6 for LTL lasso witnesses, avoiding reliance on one canonical answer string.
Initializes actual and placeholder rows from two fixed symbol embeddings and copies the remaining weights into the restricted EP-DP-CP architecture.

evaluations.setting: Propositional satisfying partial-assignment generation and LTL lasso-witness generation with normal 800k, renamed/canonicalized 800k, and reduced 80k training sets; training formulas have at most 5 APs and length 35.
evaluations.metric: External-validator correctness and exact string match on the main test set.
evaluations.result: Proposal reaches 98.03%/60.96% propositional and 98.24%/79.65% LTL on renamed data; on reduced data it reaches 70.43%/35.81% and 93.46%/68.63%, outperforming alpha-renaming and random dual embeddings in each matched regime.
evaluations.baseline: Fixed full-vocabulary Transformer, fixed embeddings with alpha-renaming training, and prior random dual-part interchangeable embeddings.

evaluations.setting: All alpha-equivalent permutations for 1,000 sampled test items per specialized model (100 for GPT-5.2), at 3, 4, and 5 APs.
evaluations.metric: Alpha-covariance: one minus the normalized number of unique de-renamed predictions.
evaluations.result: Proposal scores 100% for all task/training/AP combinations; other specialized methods range from 10.65% to 99.60%, while GPT-5.2 falls to 1.03% at 5 APs on propositional logic and 77.56% on LTL.
evaluations.baseline: Normal full-vocabulary, renamed fixed-embedding, alpha-renaming, random-embedding, and GPT-5.2 predictions.

evaluations.setting: OOD heatmap grid extending formula length from training maximum 35 to 50 and AP count from 5 to 10, with at most 100 examples per cell and unchanged operator distribution; best model selected on a separate labeled 10-AP validation set.
evaluations.metric: Mean validator accuracy over heatmap cells and accuracy by AP-count/length cell.
evaluations.result: Propositional logic: proposal 95.05%, full vocabulary 84.41%, alpha-renaming 69.96%, random embedding 77.70%. LTL: proposal 90.47%, full vocabulary 92.82%, alpha-renaming 90.13%, random embedding 87.70%.
evaluations.baseline: Prior full-vocabulary, alpha-renaming, and random-embedding models on the same heatmap.

evaluations.setting: Exhaustive attention-component ablations selected and evaluated for propositional logic and LTL, with 5-AP validation, 10-AP validation, and OOD heatmap results.
evaluations.metric: Heatmap validator accuracy and parameter count.
evaluations.result: Best scores are 95.05% (EP-DP-EA-DA-CP) and 90.47% (EP-DP-EA-CP). Replacing per-stream cross-attention with aggregate cross-attention collapses to 28.51%/20.93%; adding aggregate cross-attention slightly hurts both; decoder aggregation helps propositional logic but hurts LTL.
evaluations.baseline: Best per-task configuration with individual components added, removed, or replaced.

evaluations.setting: GPT-5.2 via Responses API, medium reasoning, low verbosity, four-shot infix prompts, deterministic temperature, JSON schema for propositional outputs; financially reduced evaluation sizes.
evaluations.metric: Validator correctness, exact match, alpha-covariance, heatmap accuracy, latency, and specialized-model top-N beam accuracy.
evaluations.result: GPT-5.2 gets 99.73% propositional and 86.83% LTL correctness in Table 1, and 99.49%/81.45% on heatmaps. The proposal reaches 99.03% top-10 and 99.54% top-25 propositional accuracy; GPT averages about 37 seconds over 387 sequential LTL samples.
evaluations.baseline: Single-response GPT-5.2 versus local specialized models, with unmatched sample counts, candidate counts, and hardware.

evaluations.setting: Conversion of a fixed-embedding 5-AP task-specific Transformer to the no-aggregate EP-DP-CP model, followed by one or five fine-tuning epochs.
evaluations.metric: 5-AP validation, 10-AP validation, and OOD heatmap validator accuracy.
evaluations.result: Propositional converted one/five-epoch models score 87.54/90.55%, 67.17/68.78%, and 70.11/71.35%; scratch scores 91.47%, 69.97%, 72.35%. LTL converted models score 94.75/95.12%, 92.44/92.02%, 85.91/85.88%; scratch scores 94.77%, 91.34%, 84.13%.
evaluations.baseline: Original fixed-vocabulary pretrained model in distribution and the same restricted architecture trained from scratch.

evaluations.setting: Scalable-copy task trained on 10 million random strings of length 20-80 with vocabulary up to 20; plus inference cost profiling on one NVIDIA L40S and LTL batch-memory profiling.
evaluations.metric: Copy edit distance, milliseconds per sample, and activation GB.
evaluations.result: All copy methods achieve edit distance 0, so the task saturates. Proposal time rises from 3.38 ms to 5.13 ms from 1 to 10 APs; LTL activation memory rises from 1.9 to 3.9 GB from 5 to 10 APs at batch 64, versus 3.1 to 3.2 GB for full vocabulary.
evaluations.baseline: Prior random embeddings and full-vocabulary models; standard O(L^2) attention versus the proposal's O(SL^2).

limitations: Author-stated: time is O(SL^2) and activation memory O(SLd); only S<=10 is evaluated, while code and theorem proving may contain hundreds of symbols.
Author-stated: dropping or gating streams can break the alpha guarantee if selection depends on token identity.
Author-stated: the method cannot generate a fresh interchangeable symbol absent from the input because no stream exists for it.
Author-stated: 'open vocabulary' means bounded extrapolation beyond the training symbol set, not an unbounded practical vocabulary.
Reviewer: the interchangeable partition and symmetry relation are supplied, not learned; scoped variables, capture-avoiding substitution, typed names, and overloaded identifiers are not modeled.
Reviewer: the sequence-level theorem omits decoding tie-breaking/randomness and numerical implementation details.
Reviewer: configuration selection sees labeled 10-AP validation examples, the maximum target AP count, so zero-exposure vocabulary extrapolation is not demonstrated.
Reviewer: proposed and standard baselines differ in training preprocessing, dimensions, heads, feed-forward width, parameter count, and sometimes data augmentation.
Reviewer: no random-seed count, uncertainty interval, significance test, or compute-matched training budget is reported.
Reviewer: experiments are synthetic formal tasks; broad claims about code, theorem proving, and general open-vocabulary learning remain unsupported.
failure_modes: Replacing corresponding per-stream encoder-decoder cross-attention with aggregate cross-attention catastrophically drops heatmap accuracy to 28.51% on propositional logic and 20.93% on LTL.
Removing decoder per-stream attention drops propositional heatmap accuracy from 95.05% to 46.55%, showing stream identity can be lost.
Aggregated decoder attention slightly hurts LTL, and adding aggregate cross-attention slightly hurts both tasks; not every symmetry-preserving component helps.
The LTL task remains dominated by temporal reasoning and full vocabulary slightly outperforms the proposal on the OOD heatmap.
The copy benchmark saturates at perfect edit distance for every method and cannot discriminate architectures.
The converted propositional model remains below both its original fixed-vocabulary in-distribution accuracy and the restricted scratch model after five epochs.
With no interchangeable input token, the dummy-stream edge case cannot emit any interchangeable output token.
A constant but wrong output can receive perfect alpha-covariance, so consistency must never be used alone.
Memory roughly doubles from 5 to 10 APs and becomes prohibitive as distinct symbol count grows.
General LLMs and fixed-vocabulary models change outputs under semantics-preserving renamings, with GPT-5.2 propositional covariance falling to 1.03% at 5 APs in the reduced audit.
reusable_insights: Dynamic per-entity streams with shared weights are a constructive recipe for equivariance when entity names are arbitrary but identity relations matter.
Separate identity-preserving paths from permutation-invariant aggregate paths; averaging everything destroys the correspondence needed for symbolic generation.
Route fixed-vocabulary outputs by symmetric pooling and entity outputs by the matching entity stream to preserve output equivariance.
Test symmetry with both semantic correctness and de-transformed consistency; neither metric subsumes the other.
Report invariant versus equivariant terminology precisely: symbol-valued predictions should transform with a renaming.
OOD model selection should not use labels at the exact held-out cardinality when the claim is zero-shot cardinality generalization, or should be labeled explicitly as OOD-aware selection.
For dynamic-stream architectures, report accuracy, wall time, activation memory, and parameter count as functions of entity count, not just sequence length.
A conversion path can reuse fixed-model weights, but comparisons should distinguish recovery of original in-distribution skill from matching a scratch dynamic model.
Synthetic formal validators are valuable because multiple outputs are valid; exact match should remain diagnostic rather than the primary metric.
open_questions: Can the architecture preserve alpha-equivalence for lexically scoped and typed binders while preventing variable capture?
Can a model infer which tokens are interchangeable rather than receiving V_i as task metadata?
How can fresh-symbol streams be allocated dynamically during decoding without breaking equivariance?
Can sparse or top-k stream routing reduce O(SL^2) time while selecting by an identity-invariant criterion and retaining the theorem?
Does the advantage persist when all baselines use identical training data, dimensions, parameters, seeds, and OOD-blind hyperparameter selection?
What performance remains when architecture selection uses only <=5-AP validation and the first exposure to 6-10 APs is final testing?
How stable are the reported gains across seeds and random formula generators, especially where differences are below one point?
Can the proof be extended formally through autoregressive sampling, beam search, masks, batching, and floating-point implementation?
Does the design scale to real code, proof terms, or algebra with hundreds of local names and mixed interchangeable/non-interchangeable identifiers?
Can a general pretrained LLM be converted without discarding aggregate capacity, and does it retain its original language competence?

competitive_landscape.title: Interchangeable Token Embeddings for Extendable Vocabulary and Alpha-Equivalence
competitive_landscape.relationship: Immediate predecessor by one of the same authors; defines interchangeable tokens and alpha-covariance and supplies the random dual-part embedding baseline and core logic/copy evaluations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Işık et al. combine a shared learned semantic component with a fresh random identity component, producing favorable but not exact covariance. The present paper replaces stochastic identity embeddings with dynamic actual/placeholder streams and symmetric attention/projection, proves equivariance, achieves empirical 100% covariance, and adds conversion and propositional evaluations. The task framing, metric, datasets, and major baseline are therefore inherited rather than new.

competitive_landscape.title: Renamer: A Transformer Architecture Invariant to Variable Renaming
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior architecture explicitly guaranteeing invariance to semantics-preserving variable renaming.
competitive_landscape.difference: Renamer represents tokens through a view mapping and referent relation and proves renaming invariance for code/system tasks, reporting 24.79-52.8% lower CPU-simulation error than a vanilla Transformer. The present method instead creates one dynamic stream per symbol, supports equivariant symbol-valued sequence generation and post-training vocabulary expansion, and evaluates propositional/LTL witnesses. Its broad claim that current architectures lack a principled renaming mechanism must be narrowed in light of Renamer.
competitive_landscape.source_version: OpenReview AilSfYM8wN, NeurIPS 2023 ML4Systems Submission 36 poster manuscript (published 2023-10-28; last modified 2023-12-12)

competitive_landscape.title: Property Invariant Embedding for Automated Reasoning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Early direct antecedent for label-invariant formula representations and unseen-symbol generalization in automated reasoning.
competitive_landscape.difference: Olšák et al. remove original labels from graph-neural formula encodings and recover structural meaning through graph links, evaluating theorem proving, premise selection, and symbol guessing. The present paper is a sequence Transformer with explicit interchangeable-token metadata, dynamic generation streams, and a formal stream-permutation argument; it does not tackle theorem-prover scale or infer symbol structure from formula graphs.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploiting Code Symmetries for Learning Program Semantics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct architectural antecedent using group-theoretic, provably equivariant self-attention for semantics-preserving code transformations.
competitive_landscape.difference: SymC derives a permutation group from program-dependence-graph code symmetries and builds equivariant attention for five program-analysis tasks. The present paper handles a simpler supplied global permutation of interchangeable tokens, supports dynamic output names and logic witnesses, and uses parallel streams; it does not encode real program dependence or scoped code symmetries.

competitive_landscape.title: Permutation Equivariance of Transformers and Its Applications
competitive_landscape.relationship: Theoretical Transformer-equivariance antecedent covering token and feature-coordinate permutations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Xu et al. show broad inter-/intra-token permutation equivariance already present in many vanilla Transformers and apply it to split-learning privacy and authorization. Their group action permutes sequence/representation coordinates, not arbitrary semantic symbol identities embedded as names. The present architecture constructs a different group action over dynamic symbol streams and symbol-valued outputs.

competitive_landscape.title: The Larger They Are, the Harder They Fail: Language Models do not Recognize Identifier Swaps in Python
competitive_landscape.relationship: Evaluation antecedent demonstrating failure under semantics-preserving identifier changes.
competitive_landscape.difference: Miceli-Barone et al. swap familiar Python identifiers in pretrained LLM prompts and document inverse-scaling failures; they propose no invariant architecture and focus on code names whose lexical meaning may matter. The present paper enforces symmetry by construction for synthetic tokens declared fully interchangeable and cannot yet establish robustness on real identifiers.

competitive_landscape.title: How Do Transformers Learn Variable Binding in Symbolic Programs?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Task-and-mechanism antecedent for systematic variable identity tracking in ordinary Transformers.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. show that a standard Transformer can learn residual-stream addressable memory and specialized heads for dereferencing assignment chains, using causal interventions. The present paper supplies an architectural identity prior and formal renaming equivariance for generation rather than explaining a learned mechanism; it has not compared against a standard model trained until systematic binding emerges.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Large Language Models Robust in Understanding Code Against Semantics-Preserving Mutations?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current evaluation competitor for prediction and reasoning stability under variable renaming and four other semantics-preserving code mutations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Orvalho and Kwiatkowska test nine pretrained LLMs on LiveCodeBench/CruxEval, include expert reasoning audits, and report drops up to 70%; they do not modify the architecture. The present paper guarantees one exact symmetry on synthetic logic but neither assesses natural-code reasoning nor other transformations, so the works address complementary robustness scope.

competitive_landscape.title: When Names Disappear: Revealing What LLMs Actually Understand About Code
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current naming-ablation benchmark antecedent separating structural semantics from human naming cues.
competitive_landscape.difference: Le et al. introduce semantics-preserving obfuscations and ClassEval-Obf and show both intent and execution tasks exploit naming shortcuts. The present paper assumes names are semantically empty and enforces that prior architecturally; it therefore does not cover domains where names legitimately carry intent, underscoring that identifying V_i is application dependent.

competitive_landscape.title: Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: General architectural antecedent for shared attention plus permutation-invariant aggregation over unordered entities.
competitive_landscape.difference: Set Transformer maps unordered set elements with permutation-equivariant attention and invariant pooling, including inducing points for efficiency. The present method must preserve distinct symbol identity and produce equivariant symbol sequences, so it uses per-symbol streams and asymmetric projection rather than reducing all entities to one invariant set representation.
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR 97, ICML 2019 proceedings, pp. 3744-3753 (fixed archival record)

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a novel Transformer mechanism that is provably invariant to renaming interchangeable tokens, generalizes to symbols unseen in training, achieves perfect alpha-covariance and improved logic-task accuracy, and can retrofit pretrained models with minimal fine-tuning.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives explicit embedding, aggregate-attention, decoder, and projection algorithms; proves that alpha-renaming permutes streams and yields a correspondingly renamed output; and evaluates full/reduced data, AP/length OOD grids, attention ablations, GPT-5.2, runtime/memory, and a conversion initialization.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the particular actual/placeholder parallel-stream Transformer and dynamic projection that combine exact symbol-name equivariance, output identity preservation, and post-training cardinality expansion on propositional/LTL sequence generation. The broad problem and several ingredients are prior: property-invariant formula graphs (1911.12073), Set Transformer aggregation, Renamer's guaranteed variable-renaming architecture, SymC's equivariant code attention, and especially the same authors' interchangeable-token formulation, alpha-covariance metric, random-embedding baseline, and logic/copy datasets (2410.17161). The claim should say equivariant rather than invariant for symbol-valued outputs and should not imply the first principled renaming architecture. Empirical novelty is further narrowed by 10-AP OOD-aware model selection, unmatched data/model capacity, saturation on copy, no LTL heatmap win, no uncertainty, and a conversion study limited to a small task-specific no-aggregate Transformer.
